title: Works, Authors and Themes: Homérosz eposza, Goethe Faustja

sections.title: Framing European Literary Masterworks
sections.content: You know the possessive *-a/-e/-ja/-je* from earlier units. It links a work to its author or theme: *Homérosz eposza* (Homer's epic), *Goethe Faustja* (Goethe's Faust), *a tudásvágy megtestesítője* (the embodiment of the thirst for knowledge). The table lists the works of this lesson.

sections.title: The works of this lesson (explained)
rows: Ancient Greek epics: the Iliad depicts the siege of Troy and Achilles' wrath; the Odyssey chronicles Odysseus' 10-year perilous journey home to Ithaca.
William Shakespeare: Rómeó és Júlia, Hamlet
English Renaissance tragedies: Romeo and Juliet portrays young lovers torn apart by family hatred; Hamlet explores moral duty, revenge, and conscience ('Lenni vagy nem lenni').
17th-century French classicist comedies exposing human greed (Harpagon) and religious hypocrisy (Tartuffe) with sharp wit.
18th-century French Enlightenment philosophical satire questioning blind optimism ('minden a lehető legjobb világon') through Candide's misadventures.
German dramatic poem: the ageing scholar Faust makes a wager with Mephistopheles (the devil) in search of ultimate knowledge and meaning. Imre Madách's The Tragedy of Man is often compared with it.

items.english: Homer's two epics, the Iliad and the Odyssey, are among the oldest works of European literature.
